summary: The splitmix64 scramble is CORRECT and it DOES decorrelate -- I reproduced the row's numbers exactly (naive seed*3+k: BOTH=4778 on draw 1 of 100,000 at p=0.05; scrambled: BOTH=253/228/251/260/261 on draws 1/2/3/20/50 against ~250 expected, all three pairs within noise, zero collisions in the effective 48-bit Random state over 600,000 (seed,stream) pairs). The Faults guard also rejects NaN and both infinities correctly. The putIfMatch landing fix is genuinely pinned -- deleting the delegate write fails exactly one test. What is wrong is elsewhere. (1) The per-class-stream property the code and the row both assert is still FALSE whenever a fault fires: the early throw skips the downstream classes' draws, so toggling `unreachable` on moved the other two classes' fault positions in 2000 of 2000 seeds. The p==0 early return was removed; the fault-fires early exit was not, and that is the same aliasing defect one step in. (2) Three of the four fixes this round exists for are unpinned: I measured `scramble` reverted to `seed*3+stream`, and the round-1 defect (one shared Random plus the p==0 early return) reinstated verbatim, and the whole range/NaN guard disabled -- all three leave the six staged tests GREEN. (3) The backlog row is marked **done** while claiming artifacts that the split removed from the commit, and defers its unmet acceptance criteria to M4.16, which is not a row anywhere in the repository. On the cost lens: nothing here changes any production request rate -- the decorator is test-only over MemoryBinStore, and put/getRange/multipart/delete inject nothing exactly as the row states.

findings.line: 73-80 (the javadoc claim), 134-137 and 138-147 (the two early throws), 151 (the skipped draw); restated at docs/internal/product/backlog.md:265
findings.finding: The stated property -- 'ONE STREAM PER FAULT CLASS, drawn UNCONDITIONALLY ... so a disabled class consumes its own stream and no other class's fault positions move' (73-80), and 'DRAWS EVEN WHEN p == 0' (123-126) -- holds only for the p==0 case. Removing the p==0 early return fixed one half of the aliasing; the other half is still there. `putIfAbsent` throws at 136 when `unreachable` fires, so `ambiguousDraws` (138) and `duplicateDraws` (151) are NOT drawn on that call, and throws at 146 when `ambiguousPut` fires, so `duplicateDraws` is not drawn. Every fired fault therefore shifts the phase of every class ordered after it, permanently, for the rest of the run. MEASURED by reproducing the control flow of 131-159 exactly: comparing (u=0.0, a=0.05, d=0.05) against (u=0.05, a=0.05, d=0.05) over 200 calls, the ambiguousPut and duplicatePut fault positions differed in 2000 of 2000 seeds. Seed 1 concretely: ambiguousPut at calls [36,49,77,93,134,146,150,159,172,176,188] with unreachable off, [39,54,82,100,145,157,161,170,183,187,199] with it on -- not one position in common. The fix is three lines: draw all three unconditionally into locals at the top of the method, then branch on the booleans.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13's criterion 1 is 'each injected fault class must have at least one seed where it changes the outcome, or the simulation proves the simulator', and the method the javadoc itself names for showing it is to hold the seed fixed and toggle one class. Toggle `unreachable` on for seed 1 and the run diverges -- but ambiguousPut fired at eleven different call indices too, so the divergence cannot be attributed to `unreachable` at all. The class whose coverage is being claimed may never have changed anything; what changed was the phase of the other two. That is the exact conclusion round 2 measured and rejected for `seed*3+k`, reached by a different route, and the code and the authoritative backlog row now both assert it is closed.

findings.line: the whole file (6 tests); the unpinned production lines are FaultInjectingStore.java:84-86, 92-94, 111-116, 127-129 and 49-60
findings.finding: Three of the four changes this round was produced by are constrained by no test. All three mutations MEASURED against `:sequencer:test --tests binjava.sequencer.FaultInjectingStoreTest` on the staged tree (working copy reverted with `git checkout --` after each; staged hash unchanged): (a) replacing the whole of `scramble` (111-116) with `return seed * 3 + stream;` -- BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 6/6 green. The phase-locked seeding the row cites as MEASURED at 19x the expected coincidence rate can be reinstated with the suite silent. (b) Reinstating the round-1 defect verbatim -- one `Random` shared by all three fields (92-94) plus `if (p <= 0.0) return false;` at the top of `fires` (127-129) -- BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 6/6 green. Both prior findings on this file re-open without a single assertion moving. (c) Disabling the `Faults` range check (56) -- BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 6/6 green: nothing in the file ever constructs a Faults with a negative, >1 or NaN probability, so the guard added in response to the earlier finding, and the `check` helper, and the message, are all deletable. The three tests that DO discriminate are the two ambiguous-landing tests and the negative control; `theSameSeedInjectsTheSameFaultsSoAFailingRunIsAPermanentRegression` (101-116) constructs one store per seed and so cannot see the per-class split at all, and `aStoreConfiguredWithNoFaultsInjectsNothingAtAll` (132-144) is p=0 everywhere and so is green under a shared stream too. What is missing is one test that holds the seed and toggles a class, asserting the untoggled classes' fault index sequences are IDENTICAL (which also pins R1), one that asserts two classes do not fire in lockstep across a seed range, and one `assertThatThrownBy` per rejected probability including NaN.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone reads FaultInjectingStore, sees three Randoms derived from one seed by a five-line bit-mixer whose only justification is a comment, and simplifies it to a single `new Random(seed)` -- a plausible cleanup, since the class is 228 lines of test support and the comment reads as over-engineering. The suite stays green. M4.13 then runs 1,000 seeds, reports 'I1-I5 hold, every fault class exercised', and the report is built on one coin wearing three hats -- classes firing in lockstep on draw 1 nineteen times more often than chance, and every per-class toggle experiment invalid. Separately, a sweep that passes `Faults(-0.0001, 0.05, 0.05)` by arithmetic on a config value silently runs with the unreachable class disabled while `injected()` still shows faults firing, so an aggregate anti-vacuity assertion stays green over a range that never exercised the class it was written for -- which is verbatim the risk the class javadoc at 29-33 names as the reason the file exists.

findings.finding: The row is marked **done** and describes a commit other than this one. (a) 'LANDED AS THE HARNESS PLUS THE THREE SIMULATION TESTS THAT PASS' -- there are no simulation tests in this commit. The three that pass live in `CommitProtocolSimulationTest`, which the same row assigns to M4.20 and which is untracked. What landed is six unit tests of the injector. (b) 'Of criterion 1's five classes: duplicated in-flight PUTs and many logical pods are modelled' -- many logical pods is not modelled by anything in this diff; it is the first line of M4.20's row, status todo. (c) The row's opening sentence still enumerates the pre-split scope ('the seeded simulation harness: injectable clock, delayed writes, reordered completions, partitioned leaders, duplicated in-flight PUTs, and MANY LOGICAL PODS driven through the seam') and is the sentence a reader takes as the completion condition. (d) 'the FAULT-INJECTION LAYER only (`FaultInjectingStore`, `SimulatedClock` and their tests)' -- SimulatedClock has no test and no caller here (see R5). The verified parts of the row I checked against the code and they hold: putIfMatch gets ambiguousPut and never unreachable (192-202); put, getRange, multipart and delete inject nothing (184-190, 204-219); delayed writes and reordered completions are absent; and the 4,778-of-100,000 measurement reproduces exactly.
findings.failure_scenario: backlog.md is authoritative and is what `next-task` and `milestone-review` read. A reader at M4's completion condition sees M4.12 done and asserting that many logical pods are modelled and that three simulation tests pass, so M4.13 ('the 1,000-seed run asserting I1-I5') looks unblocked when in fact both the invariant checker and the driver it needs are todo, and the multi-pod modelling it depends on does not exist. The same row is also the evidence record for the non-negotiable-6 style claim about what the harness covers, so a reviewer of M4.13 who checks the claim against this row is told a gap is closed that is open.

findings.line: 265 ('they are M4.16's RED RECORD'), 267 ('M4.16's two deferred progress assertions'), 265 ('M4.13 owns the two missing classes')
findings.finding: M4.16 IS NOT A ROW. `grep -n '^| M4\.' docs/internal/product/backlog.md` lists M4.0, .1, .2, .3, .3b-.3q, .4, .4b, .5, .6, .6a-.6f, .7-.14, .17, .18, .19, .20, .15 -- no M4.16, and `git log -S '| M4.16 |' -- docs/internal/product/backlog.md` finds no commit that ever added one (the identifier entered the tree in d1f6eb7 as a reference inside M4.17's prose and was never given a row). This diff adds two more references to it, and they are load-bearing: they are where the three unmet acceptance criteria of a row now marked **done** are sent. AGENTS.md's Never list is explicit -- 'the ID must RESOLVE ... An unresolvable ID is the same defect one step worse: it names nothing AND there is nothing to look up' -- and names M0.20 (check-cross-refs.sh) as the gate that would catch it, which does not exist yet, so it is this review's to catch. Same shape, smaller: 'M4.13 owns the two missing classes' assigns delayed writes and reordered completions to M4.13, whose own row (line 268) is about the 1,000-seed run and says nothing about owning a fault class.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.12 is closed having deferred the two faulted-run progress assertions and the seed range to a task that does not exist, so nothing will ever be scheduled to write them and no gate will notice: `check-commit-msg.sh` only validates the ID on a commit that claims one, and no commit will ever claim M4.16. The concrete loss is the one M4.20's row already measured -- under faults, seeds commit 0-21 against a clean run's 76 and SEED 17 COMMITS ZERO AND REPORTS CLEAN. The floor that would catch that is exactly the deferred work, and it has now been filed into a hole. Meanwhile M4.13's row, if implemented as written, will not produce the two missing fault classes either, because its row was never told it owns them.

findings.finding: SimulatedClock lands with zero consumers and zero tests in this commit. `grep -rln SimulatedClock` over the sequencer module finds only the file itself and `CommitProtocolSimulation.java`, which is untracked and is M4.20. Neither staged test file mentions it. So the commit adds 49 lines of public, unexercised code whose stated justification ('Only a movable clock reaches it') is delivered by a task that is still todo, and every mutation in it -- `advance` a no-op, `millis += d.toMillis()` becoming `-=`, `instant()` returning `Instant.EPOCH` -- survives by definition. Also, `withZone` (46-48) returns `this`, so a caller that asks for a non-UTC zone gets a clock whose `getZone()` disagrees with what it asked for, which is a documented `Clock` contract violation rather than a stylistic shortcut.
findings.failure_scenario: The split was meant to leave each piece coherent alone, and this piece is not: M4.12 is reviewed and closed without anything having established that advancing the clock advances lease expiry, and M4.19/M4.20 will be reviewed against a class whose verdict already says 'reviewed'. When `advance` is later found to be off by a factor (toMillis truncating a sub-millisecond Duration to zero, so a loop that advances by 500 microseconds never expires a lease) the sweep goes quiet rather than failing, and the review that would have caught it is the one that already passed on an untested file. Either move the file to M4.20 where its first caller is, or land it with the two-line test that pins advance and instant.

findings.line: 68 (the record), and the six literals at 135, 145, 156, 170, 178, 198, 211
findings.finding: `Injected.kind` is a free-form String and the three kind names are repeated as literals at seven sites, so the set of fault classes is not enumerable from the type. The Faults javadoc at 41-48 invokes 'rung 1 of gate-design' -- make the bad state unrepresentable -- for the probability range, and then does not apply it to the thing every downstream assertion filters on. An enum with one constant per class would make 'has every class fired?' a `EnumSet` completeness check rather than a string comparison. Relatedly, `list` at 211 records the PREFIX in the component named `key`, so an `Injected` from a list fault carries a value that is not a key.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 asserts criterion 1 as `injected().stream().filter(i -> i.kind().equals("duplicatePut")).findAny().isPresent()` per class, over 1,000 seeds. One transposed character in the literal at the assertion site or at 156 makes that clause permanently false or permanently unreachable, and because the sweep aggregates over classes, the failure reads as 'this class needs a wider probability' rather than 'this string does not match'. Nothing compiles differently and nothing goes red. With an enum the same mistake does not compile.

findings.line: 88 (`injected`), 84-86 (the three Randoms), 14 and 25-27 (the determinism claims); SimulatedClock.java:24
findings.finding: The class promises 'deterministically per seed' (14) and 'a failing seed is a permanent, named regression rather than a story about a flake' (25-27), and that promise holds only under strictly single-threaded use, which is stated nowhere and enforced by nothing. `injected` is a plain `ArrayList` mutated from every store method; the three `Random`s are thread-safe individually but their draw ORDER, which is what the seed determines, is not; and `SimulatedClock.millis` (24) is a non-volatile long written by `advance` and read by `millis()`. The row's justification for the missing fault classes -- 'pods take turns rather than running concurrently' -- is exactly the assumption, and it lives in the backlog rather than in the class.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 needs 1,000 seeds under 60s in T1 and the obvious lever is JUnit parallel execution or a parallel stream over seeds. Two seeds sharing nothing is fine, but the first person who parallelises the pods WITHIN a seed -- or reuses this decorator for M4.11's ack-ordering work, which is about pipelining and therefore about concurrency -- gets interleaved draws from the three streams and a run that is no longer reproducible from its number, plus an `ArrayList` losing or corrupting entries under concurrent add. The symptom is a seed that fails once and passes on replay, which is precisely the flake this file's javadoc says it exists to prevent, and the person debugging it will trust the javadoc.

findings.finding: `putIfAbsent` materialises the entire body into a `byte[]` and re-wraps it on EVERY call including the no-fault path (148-150), because the duplicate branch at 157 may need to replay it, while `putIfMatch` passes the caller's `Body` straight through on its no-fault path (201). So the clean baseline the simulation compares faulted runs against is not the undecorated path for putIfAbsent and is for putIfMatch: a `Body` whose supplier is single-use, or whose declared `length` disagrees with the bytes its stream yields, behaves differently through the decorator than through the raw store, and only for one of the two conditional writes.
findings.failure_scenario: A future commit -- M4.7's batching, or the multipart path -- introduces a Body whose length field is computed rather than measured. Through `putIfMatch` the store sees the original Body and the mismatch surfaces; through `putIfAbsent` the decorator has already replaced the length with `bytes.length`, so the same bug is invisible in the simulation and appears only in production against a real object store, which rejects a Content-Length mismatch. The asymmetry also means `Faults.none()` is not a true negative control for putIfAbsent, which is the one thing the test at 132-144 is there to establish.
